lessons.title: Positioning a Portfolio Across Commodity Cycles: Correlation, Hedging, and Sizing

children.text: Commodities Are Insurance, Not a Second Equity Sleeve

You can now diagnose where a cycle stands and know which instruments actually deliver exposure to it. The last question is the most practical one: how much, and against what specific risk. This final lesson brings together the correlation behaviour, sizing conventions, and hedging logic that should decide how commodities fit into an Indian portfolio, not as a second growth engine, but as insurance against risks your equity holdings can't cover on their own.

body.text: Commodities belong in a portfolio as insurance against risks your other assets can't cover, not as a growth engine competing with equities for the same job.

children.text: How Gold, Oil, and Metals Actually Correlate

Chapter 3 already flagged that gold tends to be countercyclical while oil and industrial metals tend to be procyclical. That difference is exactly what determines each one's role in a portfolio, and it's worth being precise about, since none of these correlations are fixed constants.

cells: Often low or negative correlation during risk-off, crisis-driven selloffs; can turn positively correlated during broad, liquidity-driven 'everything rallies'
The closest thing in this course to a genuine diversifier and crisis hedge
Generally procyclical with global growth, but can spike on geopolitical shocks even as equities fall
Part growth exposure, part occasional geopolitical hedge, but an imperfect and inconsistent one
Closely tracks the global growth and China industrial cycle; the most procyclical of the three
The least defensive of the three; behaves more like a growth-sensitive equity sector than a hedge

body.text: This is why gold, not oil or metals, does the heavy lifting whenever this course has referred to commodities as a 'macro hedge'. Oil and industrial metals are cyclical growth exposures that happen to sit outside the equity market, not true diversifiers away from it.

children.text: Sizing: How Much Is Usually Considered Enough?

body.label: Commonly Cited Gold Allocation Range
body.context: A frequently cited illustrative range among wealth advisors and portfolio models for gold's role as a hedge, not a rule. The right number for any individual depends on their goals, other assets, and risk tolerance.

children.text: Oil and industrial metals exposure, held through the equity proxies covered in Chapters 2 and 4, is usually sized far smaller and treated as a tactical or satellite position rather than a core holding. This isn't only about risk appetite: every proxy in this course, OMCs, upstream producers, Tata Steel, Hindalco, Vedanta, carries company-specific baggage on top of the commodity bet, which is a reason for deliberate position discipline, not just caution for its own sake.
Match the Commodity to the Risk You're Actually Hedging
Want general inflation protection? Gold and broad commodities have historically helped, though with real lags and an imperfect, non-mechanical correlation
Want protection specifically against rupee depreciation? Gold's dollar pricing does this fairly directly, as Chapter 3's rupee-tailwind math showed

Want protection against the specific combined shock from Chapter 2, oil spiking, the rupee falling, and Indian equities selling off together? Gold's safe-haven behaviour during geopolitical stress, stacked on its rupee-linked tailwind, addresses this combination more directly than any single Indian equity proxy can

body.title: Choose the Real Hedge
body.scenario: An investor holds a portfolio invested entirely in Nifty 50 index funds. They are specifically worried about a scenario where crude oil spikes on a geopolitical event, the rupee weakens as a result, and Indian equities fall together, exactly the combined shock covered in Chapter 2.
body.prompt: Between gold, oil-linked upstream equities like ONGC, and industrial metals equities, which offers the most direct hedge against this specific combined scenario, and why do the other two fall short?
body.modelAnswer: Gold is the strongest fit. It is priced in dollars, so a weakening rupee adds to its INR-denominated return exactly as Chapter 3 showed, and it also tends to benefit from the same risk-off, safe-haven sentiment that a geopolitical oil shock triggers, meaning it can rise precisely when Nifty and the rupee are both under pressure. Oil-linked upstream equities like ONGC would likely rise with the crude price itself, but as Chapter 2 covered, windfall tax policy can cap that upside, and as an Indian-listed equity, ONGC still carries meaningful correlation to the broader Nifty selloff happening at the same time. Industrial metals equities offer the weakest hedge here: they are procyclical and growth-correlated, so they would likely fall alongside the broader market rather than offsetting it.

body.text: This course has built a framework for reading and reasoning about commodity cycles, not a set of personalised recommendations. Allocation ranges, correlation patterns and hedging logic discussed throughout are illustrative and historical, not guarantees of future behaviour, and any actual portfolio decision should account for your own goals, time horizon and risk tolerance, ideally with a qualified advisor.

points: Gold is the one commodity in this course that behaves as a genuine diversifier, often moving against equities during stress, while oil and industrial metals are largely procyclical growth exposures that happen to sit outside the stock market.

A commonly cited illustrative range for a gold hedge allocation is roughly 5% to 15% of a portfolio, while oil and metals equity proxies are typically sized smaller, as tactical positions given the company-specific baggage covered throughout this course.

Match the commodity to the specific risk you're hedging: general inflation, specific rupee depreciation, or the combined oil-rupee-equity shock from Chapter 2, since gold, oil and metals do not hedge the same risks equally well.

Across all five chapters, the same idea has repeated in different forms: understanding a cycle is necessary but not sufficient, since every real-world instrument for accessing it adds cost, correlation quirks, or company-specific baggage that the underlying commodity itself does not have.
